---
title: "Fuzzy Logic: Giving a Boundary Width"
---

A thermostat can switch on at exactly $25\,^\circ\mathrm C$. The rule is crisp: just below the threshold it is off; at the threshold it is on.

The description “warm enough” can have a different purpose. We may want nearby temperatures to fit it to nearby degrees.

Fuzzy logic gives that graded description a mathematical form.

## 🔰 Define membership before calculating with it {#sec-sample-fuzzy-logic-define-membership-before-calculating-with-it}

Let $\mu_{\mathrm{warm}}(x)$ describe how well temperature $x$, in degrees Celsius, fits “warm enough” for a chosen task:

$$
\mu_{\mathrm{warm}}(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x\leq20,\\
(x-20)/10,&20<x<30,\\
1,&x\geq30.
\end{cases}
$$

At $26\,^\circ\mathrm C$, the membership is $0.6$.

The thresholds and slope express our chosen meaning of the phrase. A plant nursery and a swimming pool may require different definitions. The model can be explicit even when its concept has a gradual boundary.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sample-fuzzy-boundary
#| fig-cap: "A crisp predicate and a graded description of the same temperature axis. The membership curve is an explicit modeling choice."
#| fig-alt: "A step at 25 degrees is compared with a membership ramp from zero at 20 to one at 30. At 26 degrees the fuzzy membership is 0.6."
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

temperatures = np.linspace(15, 35, 401)
membership = np.clip((temperatures - 20) / 10, 0, 1)
crisp = (temperatures >= 25).astype(float)
figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5), layout="constrained")
axis.step(temperatures, crisp, where="post", label="At least 25 C", color="#82929B")
axis.plot(temperatures, membership, label="Warm enough: chosen grade", color="#236B8E")
axis.scatter([26], [0.6], color="#A54B30", zorder=3)
axis.annotate("(26, 0.6)", (26, 0.6), xytext=(27, 0.45))
axis.set(xlabel="Temperature in degrees Celsius", ylabel="Truth or membership grade", ylim=(-0.05, 1.1))
axis.legend(frameon=False)
axis.grid(alpha=0.15)
plt.show()
```

## 🏵 Probability and membership answer different questions {#sec-sample-fuzzy-logic-probability-and-membership-answer-different-questions}

Suppose the temperature is known to be exactly 26 in our model. Its membership in “warm enough” is still $0.6$.

That number does not say there is a 60% chance that the temperature is 26, or that 60% of thermometers will report warmth. It evaluates the description for a given input.

A probability model could separately describe our uncertainty about the temperature. We may need both a distribution over possible temperatures and a membership rule that evaluates each one.

Sharing the interval $[0,1]$ does not make the meanings interchangeable.

## ⚙️ Choose a family of connectives {#sec-sample-fuzzy-logic-choose-a-family-of-connectives}

A common introductory choice is

$$
\operatorname{NOT}(a)=1-a,\qquad
\operatorname{AND}(a,b)=\min(a,b),\qquad
\operatorname{OR}(a,b)=\max(a,b).
$$

These extend the Boolean truth tables at zero and one. Other valid families exist; for example, product conjunction uses $ab$ with its dual disjunction $a+b-ab$. The choice affects how partial grades combine. These conventions are described in [MathWorks' foundations of fuzzy logic](https://www.mathworks.com/help/fuzzy/foundations-of-fuzzy-logic.html).

For membership grades $0.6$ and $0.8$:

- Minimum conjunction gives $0.6$.
- Product conjunction gives $0.48$.
- Maximum disjunction gives $0.8$.
- The product family's disjunction gives $0.92$.

Both families agree on Boolean inputs. They express different behavior between the endpoints.

## 💡 Some familiar identities change {#sec-sample-fuzzy-logic-some-familiar-identities-change}

With minimum AND and the complement $1-a$,

$$
\min(0.6,1-0.6)=0.4.
$$

A description and its graded complement can both fit partially. Their conjunction need not be zero.

This tells us which laws survived the extension. It does not turn a partially fitting description into a contradiction in the underlying measured value.

Membership grades stay in $[0,1]$. Applying $1-a$ to $a=2$ is ordinary subtraction, but it is outside this membership contract. A missing measurement also needs explicit handling; assigning it grade $0.5$ would add a meaning we have not justified.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-fuzzy-logic-try-the-idea}

A reading has grade $0.7$ in “warm enough.” Under the minimum/maximum family, find its complement and the conjunction with its complement. Does either number describe the frequency of cold days?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-fuzzy-logic-work-it-through}

The complement is $0.3$ and the conjunction is $\min(0.7,0.3)=0.3$. Both evaluate descriptions at this reading. Frequencies of days require observations or a probability model over days.
:::
